explain.say: As a toe touches down, millions of microscopic hairs on its pads press on the surface, and a tiny pull along it makes them grip. Weak attractions between molecules, called van der Waals forces, add up to hold the gecko on.

explain.say: To lift the foot, the gecko curls its toes up from the tip, peeling the hairs off at an angle like tape, so letting go takes almost no effort. That is how some geckos can run up a wall at close to a metre a second.

faq.a: Gecko toes carry millions of tiny hairs with even tinier tips. Pulled slightly along a surface, they touch it so closely that weak forces between molecules add up to hold the gecko on, with no glue or suction.
asks: Why don't geckos fall off walls?

faq.q: How do geckos unstick their feet so fast?
faq.a: The hairs grip only when pulled along the surface at the right angle. By curling its toes up from the tip, the gecko changes the angle and peels them off easily, like peeling tape.

faq.q: How fast can a gecko run up a wall?
faq.a: Some geckos run up vertical surfaces at close to a metre a second, sticking and peeling each foot in a few hundredths of a second. Asian house geckos have even been filmed running across the surface of water.
Geckos stick to most surfaces, even polished glass, but struggle on Teflon and on wet surfaces. Their feet stay clean, because dirt tends to fall off as they walk.

faq.q: What does a gecko's tail do when it climbs?
faq.a: The tail presses against the wall to stop the gecko toppling backwards when it climbs fast, and if it falls, a swing of the tail turns it the right way up in mid-air so it lands on its feet.
asks: Why does a gecko need its tail to climb?
How do geckos land when they fall?

facts: Geckos press their tails against the wall to avoid toppling backwards when climbing fast (Jusufi and colleagues, 2008).
Gecko feet are self-cleaning: dirt tends to fall off as the gecko walks (Hansen and Autumn, 2005).
